name: FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family
title: FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family
answer: FERPA gives families and adult students the right to inspect education records and to decide who else may see them. Schools generally need written consent before sharing personal information from those records, though the school official exception allows an outside company to handle records for a service the school would otherwise perform. This matters for AI because a teacher who pastes student writing, grades, or behavior notes into a free chatbot can share protected records with a company that has no agreement with the school and is not under its direct control.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The idea is that education records belong to the family, not to the school or to any vendor that happens to touch them. Parents, and students once they reach 18, can see those records and control who else sees them. The general rule is that a school cannot share personal information from the records without written consent. The school official exception creates a narrow path for outside companies that perform a service the school would otherwise do itself. The problem it solves is practical: schools need vendors, including AI vendors, but the exception keeps the family's control intact only when the school sets the terms and limits use.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the exception works through a contract that puts the company under the school's direct control for using and keeping the records. The company may use the records only for the purpose the school authorized, and it cannot sell the data or reuse it for its own products unless the school's agreement allows that. The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the same rule applies to any school that handles education records. The most common privacy mistake with AI is a teacher pasting a student's writing, grades, or behavior notes into a free chatbot. That habit shares education records with a company the school has no agreement with, and the company's terms may let it keep and use what was typed.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, and it does not present a research study, so this idea rests on practice and current guidance rather than on new research. It relies on regulatory guidance and congressional testimony. It cites the U.S. Department of Education, 2014, for the conditions that the company must be under the school's direct control and may use records only for the authorized purpose. It also cites the Senate HELP Committee, 2024, for the statement that the Education Department planned a new rule to settle unresolved enforcement questions. The text notes that FERPA's regulations were last updated in a major way in 2011, long before generative AI arrived in classrooms, and that no proposed rule had been published as of this writing.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the exception's conditions. The company must be under the school's direct control when it uses and keeps the records, and it may use them only for the purpose the school authorized. It cannot sell the data or reuse it for its own products unless the school's agreement allows that. The risk is that a teacher's free chatbot habit can bypass all of this, because the school has no agreement with that company and the company is not under the school's direct control. Decisions about consent, contracts, and permitted use stay with the school and the family, and the text notes that until FERPA is updated, more weight falls on each district's own contracts and policies.
